title: Diwali Fatigue Is Real: Why Late Nights Leave You Exhausted, and How to Reset
excerpt: Doctors trace post-Diwali exhaustion to a measurable sleep shortfall — adults need 7 or more hours a night — compounded by heavy food and broken routines, and they outline a reset that takes days.
body:
• Diwali fatigue is mainly a sleep problem: several late nights in a row leave adults well short of the 7 or more hours a night the CDC recommends for ages 18-60.
  • The shortfall is concrete — five nights of 5 hours of sleep instead of 7 is at least 10 hours of lost sleep in one festive week, before heavy food, travel and back-to-back gatherings are counted.
  • Doctors who treat post-festival patients report fatigue, bloating and digestive distress, and workplace health data showed a 5% rise in blood sugar abnormalities and an 8.9% increase in liver function irregularities immediately after festivals.
  • The reset doctors recommend is specific: return to consistent bed and wake times within days, aim for 7-8 hours of sleep, eat light fibre-rich meals, and walk briskly for 30 minutes rather than starting an intense workout.

The parties end, the guests leave, and the tiredness does not. Post-Diwali exhaustion — heavy limbs, foggy mornings, acidity and an inability to concentrate at work — is a pattern doctors say they see every festive season, and its main driver is not the sweets. It is the sleep that the festival takes first: late-night card parties and family gatherings, early-morning pujas, travel, and irregular meals that push bedtime later night after night while wake-up times stay fixed.

The arithmetic of lost sleep

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends 7 or more hours of sleep a night for adults aged 18 to 60, and defines anything under 7 hours as insufficient sleep. More than a third of US adults already report sleeping less than that on a normal schedule. A Diwali week makes the gap measurable: an adult who sleeps 5 hours a night for five nights instead of 7 has lost at least 10 hours — more than a full night's sleep — in a single week. The CDC notes that most people who tell themselves they need little sleep struggle to stay awake and function during the day, and that chronic short sleep raises the risk of obesity and several chronic illnesses over time.

India Today's Diwali fatigue coverage points to the same mechanism for festive routines: when bed and wake times shift every day, the body's sleep-wake cycle never settles, so even a long lie-in does not feel restorative. Fragmented, mistimed sleep is not the same as enough sleep.

"Festive seasons are joyful, but they often come with disrupted routines, overeating and lack of sleep."

— Dr. Sandeep Sonawane, Consultant – Internal Medicine, Kokilaben Dhirubhai Ambani Hospital, Navi Mumbai

What doctors see after the festival

Dr. Sonawane says he frequently sees patients reporting fatigue, bloating and digestive distress after celebrations. The effect shows up in workplace health data as well. Dr. Noel Coutinho, co-founder of ekincare, reported a 5 per cent rise in blood sugar abnormalities and an 8.9 per cent increase in liver function irregularities immediately after festivals, driven by festive eating patterns and disrupted sleep schedules. Preventive test bookings rose 16 per cent after the festivities, with more people opting for lipid profiles, liver tests and HbA1c panels.

Heavy meals compound the problem. Rich, fried food eaten late sits heavily overnight, caffeine and alcohol taken during evening gatherings fragment what sleep remains, and a disturbed sleep cycle affects the hormones that regulate hunger, metabolism and focus — which is why the day after a late night often brings both exhaustion and cravings.

A reset that takes days, not weeks

The recovery advice from doctors is deliberately unglamorous. Sleep comes first: prioritise 7-8 hours of quality sleep and return to consistent bed and wake times within days, because even short-term correction restores energy and concentration significantly. Cutting back caffeine and alcohol prevents the dehydration and anxiety-linked insomnia that keep the cycle broken.

Food should get lighter, not stricter. Light, home-cooked, fibre-rich meals and probiotics such as curd or buttermilk help restore gut health, and doctors caution against extreme detoxes, which stress the system further. Movement should restart gently: 30 minutes of brisk walking, stretching or yoga can restart metabolism and improve mood, while jumping straight into intense workouts can backfire. Two to three resistance sessions a week are enough to maintain muscle during the reset.

When tiredness is a warning sign

Ordinary festive fatigue should clear within days of normal sleep. Persistent acidity, unusual fatigue or sudden weight changes deserve attention rather than another week of waiting, doctors say — those are the symptoms that post-festival screening is catching. For diaspora families who celebrated Diwali across time zones this year, the same rule applies on both sides of the ocean: fix the wake-up time first, let bedtime follow, and give the body the full 7 hours it was owed all week.
